name: Save the Children (UK): advocacy and humanitarian research (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults. The two-child limit (about 7%) in the United Kingdom; the Gavi and Nutrition for Growth pledges (about 75%) and Elrha's research (about 20%) over the Gavi-eligible and crisis countries where Save the Children works, weighted towards the largest (Nigeria, the DRC, Ethiopia, Pakistan); a judgment.
summary: Save the Children UK's advocacy and awareness work (£13.5m in 2025) and Elrha, its subsidiary that funds humanitarian research (£11.2m). None publishes a measured result, so each is built from what it won or funds, with ranged judgments, and all four branches are counted at half by the shared missing-data slider: the abolition of the UK's two-child limit on Universal Credit (announced November 2025, from April 2026) as affected families' gain in log income less the payers' loss, the 2026-2030 Gavi pledges and the Nutrition for Growth commitments as the value of the extra aid net of what it displaces, and Elrha's grants as the humanitarian spending improved by studies that change practice. It comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.05-3.1), mostly from the Gavi pledges (about seven tenths of the result), then Nutrition for Growth, the two-child limit and Elrha; the result is mostly uncertainty, judgments on what campaigning adds to pledges driving it. The biggest uncertainties are how much of each win the campaigners caused and Save the Children's share of the campaigning.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Two-child limit: households affected, April 2025

source.title: Save the Children UK, Statement: new figures show 40,000 more children affected by two-child limit (on DWP statistics, April 2025)
source.quote: Almost 1.7 million children (1,665,540) are impacted by the two-child limit, in 469,780 households.

rows.explainer: Households on Universal Credit with a third or later child born after April 2017 (DWP, Universal Credit claimants: statistics on the two child limit policy, April 2025, published 10 July 2025). They gain the child element for those children from April 2026. The count grows each year; the cost below is the first year's (2026-27), set against the latest count before it.

rows.label: Two-child limit: children in the households affected, April 2025

source.title: Save the Children UK, Statement: new figures show 40,000 more children affected by two-child limit (on DWP statistics, April 2025)
source.quote: Almost 1.7 million children (1,665,540) are impacted by the two-child limit, in 469,780 households.

rows.explainer: All children in those households, from the same DWP release.

rows.label: Two-child limit: share of the households that are couples

source.title: Save the Children UK, Statement: new figures show 40,000 more children affected by two-child limit (on DWP statistics, April 2025)
source.quote: just under half (46%) are couple households

rows.explainer: From the same DWP release, as quoted by Save the Children; the rest (54%) are single-adult households.

rows.label: Two-child limit: people per affected household
rows.explainer: Children per household plus one or two adults.

rows.label: Two-child limit: people in the households that gain
rows.explainer: Everyone in the affected households shares the gain.

rows.label: Two-child limit: yearly cost of removing it, 2026-27 (pounds)

source.title: HM Treasury, Budget 2025, Table 5.1 policy decisions
source.quote: Universal Credit Child Element: Remove the two child limit from April 2026, taking 450,000 children out of poverty Spend +0m -2,365m -2,590m -2,815m -3,095m -3,235m

rows.explainer: The extra Universal Credit paid in 2026-27, the first year, rising to £3.2bn in 2030-31 as more families have a third child. The first year matches the April 2025 household count above.

rows.label: Two-child limit: yearly gain per affected household (US$)
rows.explainer: About £5,000 a year: the child element (about £3,500 a year a child) for 1.5 children per household on average, less tapering for families in work.

rows.label: Two-child limit: affected households' consumption per person, as a share of the UK average
rows.explainer: The shared judgment both Save the Children models read (facts/save_the_children.json): {{row:tcl_consumption_share}} (25-60%) of national-accounts consumption per person, for families on Universal Credit with three or more children.

rows.label: Two-child limit: consumption per person in the affected households (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: The shared UK figure (World Bank, 2024, current US$) times the share above.

rows.label: Two-child limit: gain in ln(consumption) per person per year
rows.explainer: The household's gain over its consumption, on the site's one log-income scale (as cash-income does).

rows.label: Two-child limit: value per person per year (units of value)
Two-child limit: share of its cost that comes out of other people's consumption
rows.explainer: Judgment 80% (50-100%): the Budget pays for it with higher taxes, the Motability tax-relief reform and action on fraud and error; the part recovered from fraud and error is not a loss to anyone entitled.

rows.label: Two-child limit: value lost by those who pay for it, per year (units of value)
rows.explainer: A side effect: the money comes from other households, at about the UK survey average (the scale the families' share is on, docs/normalization.md 2.14), so its loss on the log scale is the cost over average consumption per person (a small loss spread over many). About a third of the families' gain: they consume about 40% of the average per person, and part of the cost is not a loss to anyone entitled.

rows.label: Two-child limit: chance the change happens
rows.explainer: It was announced in the Budget of 26 November 2025 and takes effect in April 2026, so 1; how much of it was campaigners' doing is the counterfactual below.

rows.label: Two-child limit: years the change counts
rows.explainer: A won reform counts the site's shared years brought forward ($win_years_counted, docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Two-child limit: wait from the decision to the first payments
rows.explainer: Announced on 26 November 2025, in force from April 2026 (Budget 2025, section 5.3), first higher payments in the assessment period after: about 0.4 years (0.3-0.6).

rows.label: Two-child limit: discount for the wait
rows.explainer: At the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Two-child limit: discounted years of impact
Two-child limit: value of the reform (units of value, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The families' gain less the payers' loss, per year, times the discounted years counted. DWP expects it to take 450,000 children out of relative poverty after housing costs by 2029-30 (Removing the two-child limit on Universal Credit: impact on low income poverty levels, 4 December 2025); the log-income gain counts every family's gain, not only those crossing the poverty line.

rows.label: Two-child limit: years of Save the Children's campaigning behind the win
rows.explainer: Judgment 4 (2-8): Save the Children UK opposed the limit from its introduction in 2017 and campaigned hardest from 2023 (its 'No Limits to Childhood' campaign; Annual Report 2025, pp. 23 and 39). The win is set against these years' advocacy spending.

rows.label: Two-child limit: value per year of campaigning at 2025's spending (units of value, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The win over the years of spending behind it, scaled to 2025's budget, set against the 2025 cost.

rows.label: Gavi: pledges to its 2026-2030 strategy (US$)

source.title: Save the Children UK, Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025
source.page: A healthy start in life, p. 16 (PDF page 17)
source.quote: In the end, more than US$9 billion (£7.8 billion) was committed to Gavi’s next strategy cycle – 2026–2030.

rows.explainer: Pledged at and after the June 2025 replenishment summit, short of the $12bn target and without the US. Save the Children UK says it mobilised more than 200 civil-society organisations, held parliamentary events and drew on its work in Ethiopia, Nigeria and Sudan.

rows.label: Gavi: share of the pledges paid
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (60-100%): donor pledges to Gavi have mostly been paid, but 2025's aid cuts (the UK to 0.3% of national income by 2027) put some at risk.

rows.label: Gavi: value of a dollar Gavi spends (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure: what GiveWell takes a Gavi dollar to achieve (about twice cash).

rows.label: Share of extra pledged aid that comes out of donors' other aid
rows.explainer: Judgment 60% (30-90%): donors' aid budgets are mostly set (and in 2025 falling), so a larger pledge to Gavi or to nutrition partly comes from other aid; some is new (finance ministries topping up for a summit, multilateral and private money).

rows.label: Value of a dollar of donors' other aid, as a multiple of cash to the very poor
rows.explainer: The aid a bigger pledge displaces is donors' other aid, of no known use: the site's shared value of a dollar of a rich country's aid budget (facts/aid_value.json, about {{row:adv_aid_vs_cash}} cash, 0.4-2×: health aid at GiveWell's Global Fund and Gavi figures, humanitarian aid at a fifth of cash, other development aid at about half), the same in every model that values aid won, kept or displaced.

rows.label: Value of the other aid displaced, per dollar pledged (units of value)
rows.explainer: A side effect: the displaced aid's value, lost, at the site's value of a dollar of cash (@cash.uov_per_dollar) times the multiple.

rows.label: Gavi: years from the pledges to the middle of the spending
rows.explainer: Judgment 3 (1.5-4): pledged mid-2025 for 2026-2030, spent across those five years.

rows.label: Gavi: discount for the wait
Gavi: years of campaigning behind the pledges
rows.explainer: Judgment 2 (1-3): the replenishment campaign ran from the investment opportunity's launch in mid-2024 to the June 2025 summit and the pledges after it.

rows.label: Gavi: value per year of campaigning at 2025's spending (units of value, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Pledges paid × the value of a Gavi dollar net of the aid it displaces, discounted to when it is spent, over the campaign's years.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: commitments at the March 2025 summit (US$)

source.title: Save the Children UK, Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025
source.page: A healthy start in life, p. 16 (PDF page 17)
source.quote: At the March 2025 Nutrition for Growth Summit, Save the Children played a key role in persuading the international community to commit more than US$27 billion (£20 billion) to tackle malnutrition.

rows.explainer: Commitments by governments, donors, development banks, foundations and businesses at the Paris summit; Save the Children helped organise it and hosts the Scaling Up Nutrition Civil Society Network.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: share of the commitments spent
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (25-80%): summit commitments are a mix of new money and restated plans, many with no tracked spending; the Global Nutrition Report finds a large share of earlier summits' commitments off course or unreported.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: value of a committed dollar as a multiple of government spending
rows.explainer: Judgment 1× (0.5-2×): most of the money is domestic budgets and development-bank lending, valued at the site's shared figure for a dollar of government spending; nutrition programmes can do better than the average budget, loans and rebadged spending worse.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: value of a committed dollar (units of value)
rows.explainer: The shared value of a dollar of government spending (GiveWell) times the multiple.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: years from the commitments to the middle of the spending
rows.explainer: Judgment 2.5 (1-4): the commitments were made in March 2025 and mostly run to 2030, so the middle of the spending is about 2.5 years on; 1 if most is spent in the first years, 4 if it is back-loaded or late.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: discount for the wait
Nutrition for Growth: years of campaigning behind the commitments
rows.explainer: Judgment 2 (1-3): preparation from 2024 (the International Advisory Group) to the March 2025 summit.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: value per year of campaigning at 2025's spending (units of value, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Commitments spent × the value per dollar net of the aid displaced, discounted, over the campaign's years.

rows.label: Other campaigns' results, as a share of the three wins modelled
rows.explainer: Judgment 30% (0-100%) of the modelled wins: the other campaigns of 2025 (against the UK aid cut, on debt, child marriage costing endorsed by 54 African governments, the Comprehensive School Safety Framework's 85 endorsing governments, children in the COP30 text, online safety) had no measured result; most changed words, not money. Anchor: the annual report names about nine campaigns in 2025 (pp. 13-23), three of which moved money and are modelled; if each of the other six is worth a twentieth of an average modelled win, together they add 30%; 0 if none mattered, 100% if they are worth as much as the money wins.

rows.label: Elrha: share of its spending that is research and innovation grants
rows.explainer: Judgment 75% (60-90%): Elrha (54 staff in 2025, Annual Report p. 41) runs calls, peer review and research uptake work beside the grants.

rows.label: Elrha: cost of a research or innovation project (US$)
rows.explainer: Judgment $400,000 ($200,000-$800,000): R2HC's research grants run to a few hundred thousand pounds over two or three years; innovation grants are smaller.

rows.label: Elrha: projects funded per year (implied)
Elrha: chance a project changes what humanitarian responders do
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (3-25%): most studies confirm or refine practice; R2HC's own impact case studies name a few that changed guidelines (cholera response, mental health in emergencies). A share across many projects, not one bet.

rows.label: Elrha: humanitarian spending a year whose practice a changed study improves (US$)
rows.explainer: Judgment $20m ($5m-$100m) a year: a guideline change reaches part of one cluster's spending (health, water, protection) across several crises; total humanitarian funding is about $25bn a year.

rows.label: Elrha: improvement in the value of that spending
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (3-30%): a better protocol or targeting rule does somewhat more with the same money.

rows.label: Elrha: value of a humanitarian dollar, as a multiple of cash to the very poor
rows.explainer: The site's shared value of a dollar of humanitarian aid whose use isn't known more exactly (facts/aid_value.json): about a fifth of cash (0.05-0.8), what the site's relief models say relief does per dollar before their missing-data step, which this branch applies itself. The spending a study improves is spread over responses' health, water and protection work, so it takes the shared figure.

rows.label: Elrha: value of a humanitarian dollar (units of value)
rows.explainer: The multiple above × the site's value of a dollar of cash.

rows.label: Elrha: years from a grant to changed practice
rows.explainer: Judgment 3 (1-5): the study, its publication and its uptake into guidelines.

rows.label: Elrha: discount for the wait
Elrha: value of a year's grants (units of value, before adjustments)
rows.formula: elrha_projects * elrha_p_uptake * elrha_spend_influenced * elrha_improvement * elrha_value_per_dollar * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, $win_years_counted) * elrha_wait_discount
rows.explainer: Projects × the chance each changes practice × the spending improved × the improvement × the value of a humanitarian dollar, for the years a won change counts ($win_years_counted, as a won reform), after the wait. A year's grants against a year's spending.

rows.label: Two-child limit: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.85 (0.6-1): DWP's static microsimulation leaves out behaviour (work, take-up) and the gain is projected, not measured.

rows.label: Two-child limit: share that wouldn't have happened without the campaigning
rows.explainer: Judgment 30% (10-60%): the share of the decision due to the campaigners at all. Labour's child poverty taskforce, the strategy's targets and the fiscal room drove it; campaigners kept it on the agenda and, Save the Children says, families' testimony was 'instrumental'. Years brought forward are the shared $win_years_counted, not a second question here (Convention 5).

rows.label: Two-child limit: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Judgment 12% (5-25%): Save the Children UK's share of the campaigning resources: the End Child Poverty coalition (over 100 organisations), the Child Poverty Action Group, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, the Resolution Foundation, Action for Children, Barnardo's, the Church of England's bishops; Save the Children was one of the largest and ran its own campaign.

rows.label: Two-child limit: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: no measured effect of the campaign; the change and its value come from the Budget's costing and our judgments. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Two-child limit: adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Gavi: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.9 (0.6-1): GiveWell's value of a Gavi dollar is for its vaccine spending at today's margin; the next cycle buys more of the same.

rows.label: Gavi: share that wouldn't have happened without the campaigning
rows.explainer: Judgment 3% (1-8%) of the pledges added by civil society's campaign as a whole: donors set pledges in finance and foreign ministries against their aid budgets; advocacy moves the margin. Anchor: the 2025 pledges ($9bn) fell $3bn short of the $12bn target, with the US withdrawn; if the campaign moved a tenth of a gap of that size that donors might otherwise have left open, that is $0.3bn, 3% of the pledges. 1% if ministries had decided before the campaign, 8% if it held two or three large donors' pledges up. No study measures it.

rows.label: Gavi: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Judgment 15% (5-30%): Save the Children UK's share of civil society's campaigning (it mobilised more than 200 organisations; ONE, Global Citizen, RESULTS and other Save the Children members campaigned too).

rows.label: Gavi: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: no measured effect of the campaign on pledges. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Gavi: adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.8 (0.5-1): the value of a committed dollar is the site's average for government spending, not measured for nutrition.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: share that wouldn't have happened without the campaigning
rows.explainer: Judgment 1% (0.3-4%): most summit commitments restate planned spending; the campaign adds a little at the margin.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (3-25%): Save the Children helped organise the summit and pulled together a joint movement commitment, among many governments, the host and other groups.

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: no measured effect. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Nutrition for Growth: adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Elrha: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.7 (0.4-1): no evaluation of Elrha's portfolio's effect on practice was read.

rows.label: Elrha: share that wouldn't have happened without the campaigning
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (40-90%): other funders (Wellcome, NIHR, USAID's research arms) would fund some of the same questions.

rows.label: Elrha: Save the Children UK's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (50-90%): the researchers' institutions and partners add their own time and money to each project.

rows.label: Elrha: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: Elrha's reach and uptake are judgments, with no measured outcome. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Elrha: adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own row; this is their outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.formula: (tcl_value_per_year * tcl_total_adj * tcl_attribution_share + gavi_value_per_year * gavi_total_adj * gavi_attribution_share + n4g_value_per_year * n4g_total_adj * n4g_attribution_share + elrha_value_per_year * elrha_total_adj * elrha_attribution_share) / (tcl_value_per_year * tcl_total_adj + gavi_value_per_year * gavi_total_adj + n4g_value_per_year * n4g_total_adj + elrha_value_per_year * elrha_total_adj)
rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own row; this is their outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Share of credit used (average of the branches)
rows.explainer: The branches' average share of the resources, for reading only.

rows.label: Missing data: outcome-weighted average of the branches

rows.label: All adjustments: outcome-weighted average of the branches
rows.formula: (tcl_value_per_year * tcl_total_adj * tcl_total_adj + gavi_value_per_year * gavi_total_adj * gavi_total_adj + n4g_value_per_year * n4g_total_adj * n4g_total_adj + elrha_value_per_year * elrha_total_adj * elrha_total_adj) / (tcl_value_per_year * tcl_total_adj + gavi_value_per_year * gavi_total_adj + n4g_value_per_year * n4g_total_adj + elrha_value_per_year * elrha_total_adj)
rows.explainer: Each branch applies its own row; this is their outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Money moved or raised for other charities (US$)
rows.explainer: Save the Children UK's grants to partners are in its programmes model; the pledges its campaigns won are valued above as won policy, not as money moved, because their destinations (Gavi, governments) aren't the site's moved-money destinations.

rows.label: Money moved per dollar of the charity's cost
rows.explainer: Context, and the donors' share of the resources with credit by share of resources on.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium, Helen Keller Intl, New Incentives), each at GiveWell's figure for the charity on the rankings (its programmes and locations weighted by funding) under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: This organisation moves money only to global health and poverty charities, so a dollar moved is valued at that destination alone (GiveWell's Top Charities, live).

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).
